title: Design food delivery (DoorDash/Swiggy)
scopeHtml: Scope: requirements, API, estimates, discovery, order saga, dispatch, tracking, peak handling.

notes.title: Requirements
notes.html:
A food delivery app connects three parties: a customer who orders, a restaurant that cooks, and a rider who carries the food. DoorDash, Swiggy, Zomato, Uber Eats and Deliveroo work like this. It looks like e-commerce, but the clock is brutal: food gets cold, the restaurant's kitchen has a limited speed, and a rider must be at the right place at the right minute.

Functional requirements

  • Browse and search restaurants and menus near me (with availability, ETA, ratings).
  • Place an order: cart, price, payment.
  • Restaurant accepts and prepares; a delivery partner is assigned; customer tracks live.
  • Ratings, promotions, refunds.

Non-functional requirements

  • Search and menu browse: under 200 ms p95, heavily cached, eventual consistency OK.
  • Order placement: correct and exactly-once (no double charge, no lost order).
  • Assignment: rider found within about 1 to 2 min; ETA accuracy within a few minutes.
  • Spiky load: lunch and dinner peaks, rain, cricket match finals, IPL nights (Swiggy and Zomato report big spikes).

Decision gravity. Decide up front that the order is a long-running workflow (a saga with a state machine), not one DB transaction. It spans payment, restaurant, dispatch, which are different services and different humans. That choice is a one-way door for the data model.

Everyday analogy. A restaurant with a phone, a kitchen and a motorbike courier: the order slip travels between all three and must not get lost.

Common interview traps.

  • Treating it as plain e-commerce; ignoring the cooking time and rider logistics.
  • Forgetting the restaurant side (menu management, accept/reject, stock-outs).
  • Not asking about scale per city and number of restaurants.

notes.title: API
notes.html:
GET /v1/restaurants?lat=12.97&lng=77.59&cuisine=biryani&sort=eta&cursor=...
200 { "items": [ { "id": "r_12", "name": "...", "etaMin": 32, "rating": 4.4,
                   "isOpen": true, "deliveryFee": 25 } ], "next": "..." }

GET /v1/restaurants/r_12/menu
200 { "version": 881, "items": [ { "id":"m_1","name":"Veg Biryani","price":210,"available":true } ] }
POST /v1/cart/quote
{ "restaurantId":"r_12", "items":[{"id":"m_1","qty":2}], "address":{"lat":12.97,"lng":77.59}, "couponCode":"NEW50" }
200 { "quoteId":"qt_77", "total":472, "breakup":{"items":420,"delivery":25,"tax":27}, "validUntil":"..." }

POST /v1/orders
Idempotency-Key: 5f9d-...
{ "quoteId":"qt_77", "paymentMethodId":"pm_3" }
201 { "orderId":"o_9001", "state":"PLACED" }
409 -> price changed or item unavailable (client re-quotes)
GET  /v1/orders/o_9001            -> state, eta, rider
PUT  /v1/restaurant/orders/o_9001/accept   { "prepMinutes": 15 }   // restaurant tablet
PUT  /v1/restaurant/orders/o_9001/reject   { "reason": "OUT_OF_STOCK" }
POST /v1/rider/location           { "lat":..,"lng":.., "ts":.. }
PUT  /v1/rider/tasks/t_5/pickup | /deliver

The quoteId freezes price and tax so the customer pays what they saw. The Idempotency-Key makes retries on a bad network safe.

Industry example. DoorDash's merchant APIs (menu sync, order injection) follow this pattern; restaurants with POS integrations push menu updates, small ones use a tablet.

Everyday analogy. A signed bill: the quote is the printed total, the order is the signature.

Common interview traps.

  • Recomputing price at order time without a locked quote.
  • No idempotency key (double orders and double charges).
  • Cursor-less pagination of restaurant lists.

notes.title: Estimates
notes.html:
Assume 5M orders/day across a country (Swiggy/Zomato scale is on that order), 70% in two 2-hour peaks.

Quantity Calculation Result
Orders avg 5M / 86,400 ~58/s
Orders peak 70% of 5M in 4 h = 3.5M / 14,400 ~245/s, plan 400/s
Browse/search ~40 browse sessions per order x 5M / 86,400 x 3 (peak) ~7,000 to 10,000/s
Restaurants 300k restaurants x 100 menu items x 1 KB 30 GB of menu data
Rider pings 300k active riders at peak / 5 s 60k writes/s
Order record items, payment, events ~5 KB 5M x 5 KB = 25 GB/day, ~9 TB/year
Events per order ~15 state changes 75M events/day, ~900/s

What this tells you. Order volume is modest (hundreds per second): a sharded relational DB handles it. Browse traffic is 30x to 100x orders and read-heavy, which is a cache plus search-index problem. The location firehose is 60k/s, a lot smaller than ride hailing, because there are fewer riders and slower updates. Hard part: workflow correctness and dispatch quality, not raw QPS.

Everyday analogy. Thousands of people read the menu board for every one person who orders.

Common interview traps.

  • Sizing for ordering only and forgetting browse traffic dominates.
  • Applying ride-hailing ping numbers (millions/s) here.
  • Averaging the day instead of using the lunch/dinner peak.

notes.title: High-level design
notes.html:
Components

  • Catalog and menu service: source of truth for restaurants, menus, stock; writes in a relational DB, changes streamed into the search index (Elasticsearch/OpenSearch) via CDC.
  • Discovery/search service: geo + text + filters + ranking; reads only from the index and cache.
  • Order service: owns the order state machine and writes to the DB; emits events to Kafka (outbox pattern).
  • Payment service: authorise first, capture on delivery (or capture and refund on cancel); idempotent.
  • Dispatch service: assigns riders (geo index like in the ride-hailing design).
  • Tracking/ETA service: rider position plus prep time estimate.
  • Notification: push, SMS, restaurant tablet alert with a loud ring and retry until acknowledged.

Order state machine

PLACED -> PAID -> ACCEPTED_BY_RESTAURANT -> PREPARING -> READY
   |         |            |                              |
CANCELLED  FAILED     REJECTED -> refund        RIDER_PICKED_UP -> DELIVERED

Decision gravity. Orchestrate the order as a saga with an explicit state machine in one service (orchestration), not a chain of services each reacting to the last (choreography). Orchestration is easier to debug and to time out ("restaurant did not accept in 3 min, cancel and refund"). It breaks when the orchestrator is a bottleneck or SPOF; shard it by orderId and keep it stateless over the DB. Moving to a different pattern later is a heavy migration.

Industry examples. Swiggy and Zomato publicly describe Kafka-based event backbones and Elasticsearch for discovery; DoorDash described moving from a monolith to services with Kafka, and uses Cassandra and Postgres in the stack.

Everyday analogy. A project manager (orchestrator) who calls payment, kitchen, and courier in order and cancels everything if one fails.

Common interview traps.

  • One distributed transaction across payment, restaurant, dispatch.
  • Dispatching before the restaurant accepts (the rider waits for 20 min).
  • Letting the restaurant tablet be the only notification channel (no fallback call).

notes.title: Deep dives
notes.html:
Discovery: geo plus search plus ranking

Query: "biryani near me, open now, under 40 min". Two ingredients: restaurants that can serve this address (a serviceability check) and ranking.

  • Serviceability: each restaurant has a delivery polygon or radius (3 to 8 km, shrinking when busy). Index restaurants by geo cell (H3/geohash/S2). Customer query: look up restaurants in the customer's cell and neighbours, filter by polygon.
  • Search: Elasticsearch document per restaurant/dish with fields: name, cuisine, geo-point, open hours, rating, price band, popularity. Query is a bool with geo_distance filter plus text match plus a function_score for ranking.
  • Ranking: relevance, ETA, rating, conversion rate, promotions, personalisation. Start with a hand-tuned formula; move to a learning-to-rank model later.
  • Freshness: menu and stock changes flow into the index in seconds through CDC or events; availability (open/closed, busy) is held in Redis and checked at read time because it changes too fast for reindexing.
{ "query": { "bool": {
    "must":   [ { "match": { "name_cuisine": "biryani" } } ],
    "filter": [ { "geo_distance": { "distance": "6km", "location": { "lat": 12.97, "lon": 77.59 } } },
                { "term": { "is_open": true } } ] } },
  "size": 20 }

Decision gravity. Search index is a derived view (rebuildable), so it is a two-way door: you can change engines. The geo cell choice leaks into data and shards, which is harder to undo. Cache discovery per (cell, filters) for 30 to 60 s; it breaks when you personalise heavily (cache hit falls), so cache the candidate set and rank after.

Everyday analogy. A food court directory that only lists stalls open now and within walking distance.

Common interview traps.

  • Hitting the primary DB for browse.
  • Ignoring real-time availability, showing closed restaurants.
  • Using straight-line distance instead of road time for serviceability.

Order placement, payments and the saga

Steps for POST /orders:

  1. Validate quote (not expired, items available, prices unchanged).
  2. Insert order row PLACED with idempotency key as a unique constraint.
  3. Authorise payment (hold money, do not capture yet).
  4. On authorise success, set PAID and notify restaurant.
  5. Restaurant accepts within, say, 120 s (else auto-cancel, void the authorisation).
  6. After delivery capture the payment.

Persist state transitions with the transactional outbox: write the order row and an outbox row in one DB transaction; a relay publishes to Kafka. This avoids "order saved, event lost".

CREATE TABLE orders (
  order_id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY, customer_id BIGINT, restaurant_id BIGINT,
  state TEXT, total_paise BIGINT, idempotency_key TEXT UNIQUE,
  version INT, created_at TIMESTAMPTZ);
-- Compare-and-set the state to avoid races (restaurant accept vs. customer cancel)
UPDATE orders SET state='ACCEPTED', version=version+1
 WHERE order_id=$1 AND state='PAID' AND version=$2;

Cancel races. Customer cancels as the restaurant accepts: the compare-and-set on state and version lets exactly one win; the loser gets a clear error.

Decision gravity. Authorise-then-capture instead of charge-immediately: reversible and kinder (no refund delays), but authorisations expire after about 7 days and some payment methods (UPI, wallets) do not support it, so there you debit-and-refund. Payment details are covered in the payment system design.

Production incident pattern. Symptom: customers charged, no order shown. Metric: count of orders in PAID older than 5 min without an ACCEPTED. Cause: crash between payment and event publish. Fix: outbox plus a reconciler job that finds stuck states and acts.

Everyday analogy. Reserving a table with a card hold: the money is frozen, charged only when you finish the meal.

Common interview traps.

  • Charging first and then discovering the item is out of stock.
  • Publishing to Kafka outside the DB transaction.
  • No timeouts per state (orders stuck forever).

Dispatch: assigning the rider

Timing matters: send the rider so they arrive when the food is ready. Estimate prepTime (restaurant-reported, corrected by history per restaurant/hour; ML works well here) and travelTime (rider to restaurant). Trigger dispatch at T_ready - travelTime - buffer, not at order placement.

Choosing the rider:

  • Candidates: free or about-to-finish riders within 3 to 5 km of the restaurant (geo index).
  • Score: ETA to restaurant, ETA from restaurant to customer, rider rating, fairness (waiting time), and batching: can this rider carry two orders from the same area without making either late by more than 5 min?
  • Offer sequentially or to 2 to 3 riders; first accept wins (CAS on rider state).

Batching is a variant of the vehicle routing problem; solve approximately with greedy insertion or local search every few seconds per zone. DoorDash has described its dispatch optimisation and ML-based prep estimates in its engineering blog.

Decision gravity. Dispatch timing and scoring are policy: easy to change and A/B test (reversible). The invariant that one rider state owner uses CAS is hard to retrofit. When demand exceeds supply, the system shifts to surge-like incentives and a longer promised ETA rather than failing.

Everyday analogy. Calling the courier to arrive just as the parcel is ready, not an hour before.

Common interview traps.

  • Assigning the rider at order time (rider idles at the restaurant).
  • Ignoring batching economics.
  • Single-sourcing prep time from the restaurant with no correction.

Live tracking and ETA

Rider pings every 5 s go to a location gateway, into the geo index and a Kafka topic. Customer tracking screen gets pushes via WebSocket or server-sent events, or simple polling every 5 to 10 s (cheaper and acceptable here: only a few hundred thousand concurrent watchers).

ETA shown = remaining prep + rider travel to restaurant + wait + travel to customer, with ML correction and a buffer. Recomputed on state change and every 30 s.

Industry example. Swiggy and Zomato show the rider moving on the map with coarse smoothing; the ETA mostly changes by state transitions rather than every second.

Decision gravity. Polling vs push: polling is easier to scale and operate and is easily swapped for push later (reversible); choose push when concurrent watchers go into millions.

Common interview traps.

  • A promise that is too optimistic (ETA lower than reality hurts trust more than a longer, honest one).
  • Persisting each ping in the order DB.

Peak handling and restaurant overload

Dinner peak: 10x lunch for some cities. Protect the system with:

  • Autoscaling stateless services on queue depth and CPU; pre-scale before known events.
  • Load shedding: pause the lowest-priority work (recommendations, analytics) first.
  • Restaurant throttling: if a kitchen has more than N open orders, mark it "busy" and raise the prep time or stop accepting. This protects customer experience more than any server tuning.
  • Dynamic delivery radius: shrink radius when riders are scarce.

Everyday analogy. A restaurant that takes its name off the board when the kitchen is full.

Common interview traps.

  • Only scaling servers, ignoring the real bottleneck (kitchens and riders).
  • No degraded mode.

notes.title: What interviewers look for
notes.html:
• Scope across three actors, not only the customer.
  • Numbers: orders per second is small, browse is large, pings moderate.
  • Order as a saga/state machine with timeouts, idempotency, outbox, compare-and-set transitions.
  • Discovery design: geo plus search plus cache, serviceability, availability freshness.
  • Dispatch timing tied to prep time, batching, assignment without double booking.
  • Failure thinking: restaurant never accepts, rider cancels, payment succeeds but event lost, tablet offline.
  • Seniors add experiments and ML (prep time, ETA), cost of rider idle time, and multi-city isolation.

Common interview traps.

  • A beautiful ride-hailing clone with no kitchen in it.
  • No reconciliation job.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Three-sided marketplace: customer, restaurant, rider; the order is a saga with a state machine and timeouts.
  • Load: hundreds of orders per second, thousands of browse requests per second, tens of thousands of rider pings per second.
  • Discovery = geo cell serviceability + Elasticsearch + Redis availability + ranking; cache the candidate set.
  • Place orders with a locked quote, idempotency key, authorise then capture, outbox events, compare-and-set transitions.
  • Dispatch rider relative to predicted food-ready time, score by ETA and batching, assign with one owner and CAS.
  • Protect peaks with autoscaling, shedding and busy-kitchen throttling; reconcile stuck orders.

questions.promptHtml: Why is a food order modelled as a saga with a state machine instead of one database transaction?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The order spans payment, a restaurant (a human) and a rider; the signal is understanding long-running workflows.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: One ACID transaction cannot span a payment provider, a restaurant tablet and a rider who may take 40 minutes. So I model the order as a state machine (PLACED, PAID, ACCEPTED, PREPARING, READY, PICKED_UP, DELIVERED, plus CANCELLED/REJECTED), advance it step by step with compare-and-set, and give every state a timeout and a compensation (void the authorisation, refund). I orchestrate it from one service so timeouts and debugging live in one place.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
PLACED -> PAID -> ACCEPTED_BY_RESTAURANT -> PREPARING -> READY -> RIDER_PICKED_UP -> DELIVERED
  |         |            |
CANCELLED  FAILED     REJECTED -> refund

Orchestration (one service owns the machine) versus choreography (services react to each other's events): orchestration makes "restaurant did not accept in 3 minutes, cancel and refund" a simple timer. The orchestrator must be stateless over the DB, sharded by orderId, so it is not a SPOF.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• One distributed transaction across payment, restaurant and dispatch.
  • Dispatching the rider before the restaurant accepts.
  • No timeout per state, leaving orders stuck forever.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What if the customer cancels as the restaurant accepts? -> Compare-and-set on state and version; exactly one wins.
  2. Orchestration or choreography? -> Orchestration for debuggability and timeouts; choreography scatters the logic.
  3. How do you avoid lost events? -> Transactional outbox in the same DB transaction as the state change.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "use microservices with Kafka". Senior: state machine, compensations, timeouts, CAS, outbox.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Choreographed flows left orders in limbo after one consumer crashed; adding an orchestrator timer plus reconciler fixed it.

questions.promptHtml: What is the transactional outbox, and how does compare-and-set on order state stop races? Show the SQL.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: These two patterns are the mechanical answer to "payment succeeded but the event was lost" and "cancel versus accept".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The outbox writes the order state change and an event row in the same DB transaction, and a relay publishes outbox rows to Kafka, so I never have "saved but not published". Compare-and-set updates state only if the current state and version match, so two concurrent transitions cannot both succeed: one updates one row, the other updates zero rows and gets an error.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
BEGIN;
UPDATE orders SET state='ACCEPTED', version=version+1
 WHERE order_id=$1 AND state='PAID' AND version=$2;      -- 0 rows = lost the race
INSERT INTO outbox(order_id, type, payload) VALUES ($1, 'ORDER_ACCEPTED', $3);
COMMIT;

The relay polls (or uses CDC) and publishes with at-least-once delivery, so consumers must be idempotent (dedupe by event id). A reconciler job scans for orders stuck in a state longer than its timeout (for example PAID for over 5 minutes) and acts.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Publishing to Kafka outside the DB transaction.
  • Treating at-least-once delivery as exactly-once in consumers.
  • A reconciler that retries without idempotency.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Polling or CDC for the relay? -> Polling is simple; CDC (Debezium-style) lowers latency and load.
  2. Ordering of events? -> Per order key on the Kafka topic preserves order.
  3. What if the relay crashes after publish but before marking sent? -> Duplicate publish; consumers dedupe.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "publish after commit". Senior: the dual-write problem, outbox, idempotent consumers, reconciler.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Customers charged but with no order shown traced to a crash between the payment call and the event publish.

questions.contextHtml:
Complaints: 1,900 customers in the last hour were charged but see "waiting for restaurant". Dashboard excerpts:

orders in PAID older than 5 min: 1,873
orders in ACCEPTED:               normal
payment auth success rate:        99.2%
order-service deploy:             14:42 (new outbox relay)
kafka topic order-events:         produce errors 0.3%

Restaurants say tablets never rang.
questions.promptHtml: Diagnose and fix; what is the red herring?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Blames payment (success rate is fine) or the restaurant tablet app.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What changed at 14:42? Is the outbox row written for these orders? Is the relay lagging?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Run the reconciler manually: for orders in PAID older than 5 minutes with no ACCEPTED, republish the event (idempotent) or auto-cancel and void authorisations after the SLA.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) new outbox relay dropped rows after a Kafka produce error; (b) notification service down; (c) payment webhook issue (unlikely, auth rate fine).
  4. How I'd verify each: Count outbox rows with sent_at IS NULL and age; relay error logs; whether the notification service received events.
  5. Root cause: The relay marked rows as sent before the produce was acknowledged (or swallowed a 0.3 percent error), so events were lost though the state was committed.
  6. Fix: Mark sent only after produce ack; retry failed rows; reconcile existing stuck orders; idempotent consumers make republish safe.
  7. Prevention: Metric "orders in PAID older than N minutes", alert on outbox backlog age, a reconciler running every minute.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not charge-first-and-hope; I would not mass refund before knowing which orders the restaurant actually received (some may be cooking).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Duplicate notifications after republish? -> Consumers dedupe by event id; the tablet shows the order once.
  • Why authorise-then-capture helps here? -> Voiding an authorisation is cleaner than refunds.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A relay refactor flipped the order of "mark sent" and "publish"; the 0.3 percent error rate was dismissed as noise for three hours.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Blames payment or tablets.
  • Hire: Finds lost events and runs reconciler.
  • Strong hire: Fix ordering in the relay, stuck-state alert, safe replay, customer remediation policy.

questions.contextHtml: Average 5M orders/day, 70 percent in two 2-hour peaks. A cup final is expected to produce 10x dinner load in some cities. Browse sessions run about 40 per order. The proposal: "autoscale all services 10x". Cost budget does not allow 10x compute everywhere.
questions.promptHtml: Where is the real load, and what do you scale or throttle?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Scales everything uniformly and ignores kitchens and riders.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which cities? Can we change delivery radius and prep-time promises? How many riders are available?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Pre-scale known-event capacity, not reactive.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Peak orders: 3.5M in 4 h = 245/s, plan 400/s; at 10x in a city that is a fraction. Browse is 40x: 10k/s nationally. Rider pings 300k riders/5 s = 60k/s.
  4. How I'd verify each: Load test the browse path through cache and search index; test dispatch; watch open orders per restaurant.
  5. Root cause: Orders are modest QPS; browse is a cache/search problem; the true bottlenecks are kitchen capacity and rider supply.
  6. Fix: Cache discovery per (cell, filters) for 30 to 60 s; pre-scale search and cache; load-shed low priority (recommendations, analytics) first; restaurant throttling: if open orders exceed N mark "busy", raise prep time or stop accepting; shrink delivery radius when riders are scarce; show honest longer ETAs.
  7. Prevention: Event calendar tied to capacity, game days, per-restaurant open-order caps.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not promise optimistic ETAs: trust loss beats a longer honest estimate. I would not autoscale the DB reactively; plan its capacity ahead.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• DB write capacity at 400 orders/s? -> A sharded relational DB handles it; 25 GB/day of order records.
  • Riders not enough? -> Incentives, radius cuts, batching.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A final's night saw servers fine and customers furious: kitchens were slammed and nobody throttled them.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Uniform 10x.
  • Hire: Correct load split and caching.
  • Strong hire: Kitchen throttling, radius control, pre-scale and honest ETA policy.

questions.contextHtml:
On a flaky mobile network a customer taps "Place order" three times. Support sees 112 duplicate orders last week and 40 complaints "price changed at checkout". Current flow: POST /orders accepts items and recomputes price at the server at order time; no idempotency key.

POST /v1/orders {"restaurantId":"r_12","items":[...],"paymentMethodId":"pm_3"}
201 {"orderId":"o_9001"}
(client times out, retries)
201 {"orderId":"o_9002"}
questions.promptHtml: Redesign the API contract and explain the failure cases.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Disable the button" on the client.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: How long must a quote be valid? Which fields can change (price, tax, availability)? Which payment methods?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Dedupe window server-side: same customer, same cart hash within 2 minutes returns the existing order.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Missing idempotency and unlocked price.
  4. How I'd verify each: Group duplicates by customer and cart hash within seconds.
  5. Root cause: The server cannot distinguish a retry from a new intent.
  6. Fix: POST /cart/quote returns quoteId, total and validUntil, freezing price and tax. POST /orders takes quoteId and an Idempotency-Key; the order row has a UNIQUE constraint on the key, so a retry returns the original order. If the quote expired or an item became unavailable return 409 and the client re-quotes. Payment is authorised with the same key to the provider.
  7. Prevention: Metric of duplicate keys and 409 rate; contract tests for retries.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Quotes expiring fast annoy slow checkouts; 5 to 10 minutes balances. I would not recompute price silently at order time.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Same key different body? -> Return 422; the key is bound to the request hash.
  • Where is the key stored? -> Unique column on orders, or a key table with TTL.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A double-tap on a payment screen turned into 2,000 duplicate charges during a weekend sale before keys were introduced.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Client-side fix.
  • Hire: Locked quote, idempotency key, 409 on change.
  • Strong hire: Key bound to request hash, provider-level idempotency, metrics.

questions.contextHtml:
Rider idle time at restaurants is rising and order delivery time p90 is 52 min versus a 40 min target. Data:

avg rider wait at restaurant:   11.4 min (was 5.1)
dispatch trigger:               at ORDER_ACCEPTED
restaurant-reported prep:       12 min   actual median: 19 min (dinner)
rider travel to restaurant:     6 min

The team wants to add more riders.
questions.promptHtml: What do you change in dispatch, and what do you measure?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Hire more riders" or "make the offer faster".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is prep time from the restaurant or learnt? Do we batch orders? What is the cost of a late order versus an idle rider?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Delay dispatch trigger: send the rider at T_ready - travelTime - buffer.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) prep time underestimated by restaurants; (b) dispatch fires too early; (c) rider supply shortage; (d) restaurant overload.
  4. How I'd verify each: Compare reported versus actual prep per restaurant and hour; rider wait histogram; open orders per kitchen.
  5. Root cause: Dispatch triggered at acceptance with an optimistic prep time means riders arrive 7 minutes before food is ready.
  6. Fix: Predict prep time per restaurant, per hour and per order size (history, then ML), correct the restaurant's number, and dispatch just in time. Add batching: allow a rider to carry two nearby orders if neither is more than 5 minutes late. Score riders by ETA to restaurant, ETA to customer, fairness. Offers sequential or to 2 to 3 riders; first accept wins via compare-and-set on rider state.
  7. Prevention: Dashboards of prep prediction error, rider idle per restaurant, A/B on dispatch timing policy.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Dispatching late risks cold food if prediction errs; use a buffer. More riders would raise cost without fixing waits. Policy is reversible; rider-state ownership via CAS is not easy to retrofit.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• A restaurant lies about prep? -> Down-weight the restaurant's number via its history.
  • No rider available at the computed time? -> Dispatch earlier for that zone and show a longer promise.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Idle rider minutes dropped 30 percent after the trigger moved from acceptance to predicted readiness, with no new riders.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: More riders.
  • Hire: Just-in-time dispatch with prep prediction.
  • Strong hire: Batching economics, CAS ownership, A/B measurement, correction for restaurants.

questions.contextHtml: Finance wants to charge at order time to cut payment risk. Ops says restaurants reject 6 percent of orders after payment (out of stock), producing refunds that take 5 to 7 days and about 12,000 support tickets a month. Most customers use UPI or wallets, which do not support card-style holds, and cards authorisations expire after about 7 days.
questions.promptHtml: Choose a payment flow and defend it.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Charge first" or "always authorise" without noticing that some methods cannot.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Share of payment methods? Refund SLA by method? Chargeback exposure? Can we wait for restaurant acceptance before debiting?
  2. Immediate mitigation: For methods with holds, switch to authorise-then-capture; void on reject.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Refund tickets are driven by charge-before-acceptance.
  4. How I'd verify each: Tickets by cause; reject rate by restaurant; refund time by method.
  5. Root cause: Money moves before the restaurant commits, so rejects become refunds.
  6. Fix: Method-dependent flow: cards authorise (hold) then capture after delivery, void on reject (instant); UPI/wallet debit after the restaurant acceptance step where the provider allows a mandate/collect pattern, otherwise debit-and-refund with an instant-refund target. Reduce rejects at source: real-time stock and "busy" status, auto-cancel at 120 s. Everything idempotent with provider keys; reconcile against provider reports daily.
  7. Prevention: Metrics: reject rate, time to refund, authorisation expiries.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Authorise-capture is kinder but expiry and partial captures need handling; debit-first is simple but costly in support. I would not claim UPI supports holds; verify with the provider.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Delivery takes longer than the hold validity? -> Rare for food; for long cases re-authorise.
  • Partial refund when one item is missing? -> Capture reduced amount.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Moving card payments to authorise-then-capture cut refund tickets by a third within a month with no change in conversion.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: One flow for all.
  • Hire: Authorise/capture for cards, alternative for UPI.
  • Strong hire: Addresses reject rate at source, reconciliation, idempotency, honest uncertainty on provider limits.

questions.contextHtml:
After launching personalised ranking, restaurant list p95 rises from 140 ms to 900 ms and the search cluster CPU doubles. Users also see closed restaurants as "open". Details:

discovery cache hit ratio:   82% -> 9%
ES query p95:                60 ms -> 640 ms
is_open field refresh:       reindex every 15 min
cache key:                   (userId, cell, filters)

The team wants to add search nodes.
questions.promptHtml: What went wrong and how do you fix it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Add nodes, increase cache TTL, ignore the closed-restaurant bug.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which fields are personalised? How often does availability change? What does the cache key include?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Roll back to the shared cache key for the candidate set, rank afterwards.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) the cache key now includes userId, killing hits; (b) heavier function_score queries; (c) shard imbalance; (d) availability refreshed too slowly.
  4. How I'd verify each: Cache key cardinality, hit ratio by endpoint, ES slow log, shard sizes.
  5. Root cause: Personalisation moved into the cache key, so each user is a unique query; closed status lives in a 15 minute reindex.
  6. Fix: Cache the candidate set per (cell, filters) for 30 to 60 s and apply personalised ranking after retrieval in the discovery service; keep is_open/busy in Redis, read at query time (changes too fast for reindexing), and filter out closed restaurants before returning. Index changes via CDC in seconds for menu/stock.
  7. Prevention: Hit-ratio alert, review rule: no user-level fields in shared cache keys, canary on query latency.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Post-rank personalisation limits how far ranking can reorder the candidate set (top 200 candidates); acceptable. The search index is a derived view, so changing engines later is a two-way door; geo cell choice is not.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Serviceability? -> Restaurant delivery polygon checked against the customer's cell and neighbours.
  • A restaurant goes busy mid-session? -> Redis flag read at list time; detail page rechecks.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "small ranking tweak" put the user id into a cache key and the cluster fell over at the lunch peak; the fix was a one-line key change.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Add nodes.
  • Hire: Fixes cache key and splits candidate retrieval from ranking.
  • Strong hire: Availability in Redis, CDC freshness, hit-ratio guardrails, reversibility reasoning.
